query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 2 wt.% lanthanum (La) into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent La2O3-rich tribo-oxide film during sliding in air, which will be effective in reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in its baseline (unmodified) form.
generation.intervention: A minor compositional change by alloying with ~2 wt.% lanthanum.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in air with controlled load conditions at temperatures of approximately 25 °C (room temperature), 400 °C, and 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a La2O3-rich tribo-oxide film facilitated by the La addition.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, La assists in stabilizing and promoting adhesion of the oxide scale, while at higher temperatures the La2O3 phase forms a self-lubricating and protective layer, reducing friction and wear under oxidizing conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The La-doped alloy will exhibit a statistically lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy throughout the evaluated temperature range.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which experiences increased friction and wear outside a limited optimal temperature range due to unstable oxide formation.
generation.boundary: Evaluations are limited to an oxidizing ambient environment (air) with sliding loads applied under controlled conditions and a temperature regime ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the uniform distribution of La in the matrix and whether the 2 wt.% addition is sufficient to consistently form the desired La2O3 film across all temperatures. Additionally, potential side effects on the alloy's microstructure or phase stability have yet to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set doped with ~2 wt.% La. Conduct sliding wear tests in air under identical load and sliding speed conditions at 25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C. Characterize the friction coefficient and wear rate using sensors and profilometry, and perform surface analysis (e.g., SEM, XRD, EDS) to detect and assess the continuity and composition of the tribo-oxide film.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over sliding time at each temperature
Wear rate determined by weight loss or surface profilometry
Surface film morphology and composition (via SEM, XRD, and EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the La-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the baseline, or if a continuous La2O3-rich tribo-oxide film does not form as observed by surface characterization, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

frame.system: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy used as a sliding contact material, currently in its as-cast or wrought (baseline) state without any additional modifying phase or element.
frame.goal: Achieve a consistently low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full sliding temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C.
frame.limitation: The baseline alloy exhibits difficulty in maintaining optimal tribological performance over a wide temperature spectrum due to changes in oxidation behavior, phase stability, and surface film formation.
root_cause_cues: difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction
wear rate throughout the full temperature range
evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
Performance must be maintained across room temperature to 800 °C
Tests must include defined sliding loads and operate in air (oxidizing environment)
frame.regime: Sliding wear tests conducted under controlled loads in an air environment with temperatures varied from ambient (~25 °C) to 800 °C.
prior_attempts: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy has been used as a baseline, which has shown acceptable performance only within a limited temperature range; outside this range, oxide formation and lack of a protective tribofilm lead to increased friction and wear.
frame.understanding: How the introduction of a minor alloying addition might enable the in-situ formation of a stable, lubricious tribo-oxide film that is effective over a wide temperature span.
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount (approximately 2 wt.%) of a rare earth element such as lanthanum (La) into the CoCrFeNi matrix will promote the formation of a continuous, adherent La2O3-rich tribo-oxide film during sliding. At lower temperatures, La improves the stability and adhesion of the oxide scale, while at higher temperatures (approaching 800 °C), the La2O3 phase acts as a self-lubricating layer that mitigates wear and friction. Compared to the starting CoCrFeNi alloy, the La-doped version is expected to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates across the complete temperature range. This hypothesis is supported by prior evidence from studies on RE-doped Ni-based superalloys and other high-temperature alloys, where rare earth additions improved oxidation resistance and tribological behavior. A controlled falsification experimental design would involve preparing otherwise identical CoCrFeNi samples with and without the La addition, performing sliding tests under identical load conditions across the temperature range (e.g., room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C), and analyzing the surface film morphology and composition. If the La-doped alloy fails to form a stable La2O3 tribofilm or does not show statistically significant improvements in friction and wear performance compared to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early high-entropy/alloy tribology studies initially relied on the inherent microstructural responses (like dynamic amorphization and nanocomposite surface layer formation) to achieve low friction and wear in controlled or inert environments. However, as tests moved into oxidizing conditions and broad temperature ranges, efforts shifted toward compositional modifications that promote in-situ formation of protective oxide films. For example, the reactive wear protection study (PMC8448869) demonstrated that a deliberately formed oxide nanocomposite surface can lower wear, while later work (PMC12692809) showed that minor additions of oxide-formers (Y2O3) can refine microstructures and reduce oxidation and wear at high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, maintaining a continuous, adherent, and lubricious tribo-oxide layer across the entire sliding temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C remains unsolved. The key challenge is designing a single intervention that reliably forms and stabilizes such a film under varying oxidative conditions and sliding loads, bridging the differences in oxidation behavior between low and high temperatures.
decision.lever: introduce a minor (~2 wt.%) addition of a rare earth element, specifically lanthanum, into the CoCrFeNi matrix
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend seen in prior studies where targeted compositional tweaks (such as oxide‐forming additives) have been used to promote in-situ protective oxide layers. Lanthanum is expected to foster the formation of a continuous La2O3-rich tribo-oxide film that adheres well at low temperatures and becomes self-lubricating at high temperatures, thus addressing the critical limitation of maintaining low friction and wear throughout the full temperature range under oxidizing conditions.
